identification.summary: Public reporting on the Gatak name describes a trojan (also called Stegoloader) and the group behind it that spread through pirated-software key generators [S2][S4][S6]. Microsoft's Tempest family is used for financially motivated actors [S7]. Symantec called the Gatak group cybercriminal in nature because it found no zero-day exploits or advanced modules [S2][S3].
identification.notes: The Wheat Tempest to Gatak/GOLD equivalence could not be verified: searches found no source naming Wheat Tempest, and the Microsoft mapping file cited earlier was never seen in results, so the claim was removed. Dell SecureWorks CTU reported Stegoloader active since at least 2013 [S6]. The GOLD prefix is used by Secureworks CTU for many groups, so the bare alias GOLD is ambiguous. Stegoloader is also named Win32/Gatak.DR and TSPY_GATAK.GTK and is unrelated to the Gataka banking trojan [S4].

attribution.sponsor: Financially motivated / cybercriminal (no state sponsor identified)
attribution.basis: Symantec assessed the Gatak group as likely cybercriminal because it saw no zero-days or advanced modules, while noting the malware has capabilities that could support espionage [S2][S3]. These are vendor assessments, not government attribution. The record's FIN country field is not supported by any source seen.

objectives: Symantec said the group's motive was unclear and raised data theft as a possibility, because healthcare records are priced higher than other personal information [S2][S3]. Stegoloader is described as an information stealer [S4][S6].

targeting.notes: Symantec found 40 percent of the top 20 most affected organizations were in healthcare, that the group had previously targeted insurance heavily, and that most infections (62 percent) were on enterprise computers [S2][S3]. Symantec said the group focused on US targets but had diversified to a broad range of countries over about two years [S2][S3]. CTU's 2015 Stegoloader report associated victims with healthcare, education and manufacturing [S5][S6]. Infections come from users running key generators for pirated professional software, including backup software, so victim selection looks opportunistic rather than tailored [S2][S8].

capabilities.summary: Delivery is through websites offering software key generators; the malware is installed when the victim runs the keygen, and the fake keys do not work [S2][S8]. Stegoloader is modular: a deployment module fetches a PNG image from hardcoded URLs on legitimate sites and extracts the main module from it, and code runs from memory without landing on disk [S4][S5][S6]. Modules collect recently opened documents, installed programs, browsing history and passwords, and one steals IDA-related files [S4]. Symantec noted capabilities that could support traditional espionage, but no zero-days or advanced modules [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Earliest Stegoloader/Gatak activity
campaigns.summary: Dell SecureWorks CTU reported Stegoloader active since at least 2013, spread through pirated software and key generators, with victims in healthcare, education and manufacturing [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: CTU publishes Stegoloader analysis
campaigns.summary: Dell SecureWorks CTU published its analysis in June 2015. Coverage called it the third example in a year of malware using steganography as a detection countermeasure [S4][S5][S6].

campaigns.name: Symantec: Gatak shifts toward healthcare
campaigns.summary: Symantec reported that Gatak infections concentrated in healthcare (40 percent of the top 20 affected organizations), that the group previously targeted insurance, and that it spread through keygen sites and had widened beyond the US [S2][S3][S8].

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated Gatak/Stegoloader operators; identity and size unknown. Symantec assessed them as cybercriminal [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: Modular steganography-based stealer delivered via keygens [S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Hardcoded URLs on legitimate websites hosting PNG images carrying the payload; keygen distribution sites [S4][S6][S8]. No specific indicators are recorded here.
diamond.victim: Enterprise machines, notably healthcare, insurance, education and manufacturing, mainly US [S2][S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven; likely data theft. No political motive is stated in sources [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running pirated or cracked professional software, including backup tools [S2][S8]. Memory-resident execution [S4].

gaps: The Wheat Tempest alias mapping to Gatak and GOLD is unverified; no source found names Wheat Tempest.
Which Secureworks GOLD name, if any, corresponds to Gatak was not found; GOLD is ambiguous.
Recent activity (after 2016) was not found in searches; current status is unknown.
Operator identity, geography, monetization method and any link to ransomware or other crime are unknown.
Primary documents (Symantec blog, Secureworks CTU report) could not be opened directly; page fetches failed, so findings rely on search-result summaries of them.
Country field FIN in the record is unsupported.
